title: Landscaping Contractor — Outstanding Invoices Bridged by Personal Credit
business_context: A commercial landscaping maintenance contractor serves property managers and strata corporations but cannot cover payroll without drawing on a personal line of credit each month.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — trade services sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a commercial landscaping business reports that payroll is regularly covered by drawing on a personal credit line, despite having a full roster of maintenance contracts. Several property management clients take 60 to 90 days to pay invoices and one large strata client is 120 days overdue on $38,000.
symptoms: Owner drawing on personal credit to cover payroll every month
One strata client 120 days overdue on $38,000 invoice
Several property management clients consistently pay in 60–90 days
Bank account near zero by end of each month despite full contract schedule
misleading_signals: Contract pipeline is strong with three new signed agreements
Client relationships appear positive with no formal complaints received despite extended payment cycles
Revenue has grown 18% over the prior year
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Full debtors ledger showing outstanding invoices by client and days past due
Contract payment terms for each of the top five clients
Historical record of average days from invoice issue to cash receipt for each client

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Produce a debtors report showing all outstanding invoices sorted by age and client, then contact the 120-day overdue strata client immediately to negotiate a payment plan or enforce contract terms.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: take a business loan to cover the cash shortfall
hire more staff to win additional contracts
reduce contract rates to retain the slow-paying clients
cut staff headcount to reduce costs

must_not_claim: the business needs more clients to fix the cash problem
costs are too high relative to revenue
ideal_depth: identifies that billing terms do not align with payroll cycle
notes that no structured debtor follow-up process exists

title: Artisan Bakery — Ingredient Cost Inflation Compressing Margin
business_context: A wholesale artisan bakery supplying cafes and restaurants has seen gross margin fall from 44% to 29% over 18 months as commodity ingredient costs have risen and the owner has held pricing to avoid losing wholesale accounts.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — food production sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of an artisan bakery reports that gross profit has declined significantly over 18 months even though revenue has grown. Flour, butter, and egg costs have increased 35% but wholesale prices charged to cafe and restaurant clients have not changed. The owner fears that raising prices will cause major accounts to switch to larger industrial suppliers.
symptoms: Gross margin compressed from 44% to 29% over 18 months
Ingredient costs have increased approximately 35% across flour, butter, and eggs
Wholesale pricing unchanged for 18 months
Owner taking reduced personal drawings to cover operating shortfall
misleading_signals: Revenue has grown 12% over the same period
Order book remains full with no client cancellations
Several clients have provided positive feedback on product quality
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Cost breakdown by ingredient category showing current versus 18-months-ago costs
Gross margin by product line or product category
Competitor wholesale pricing for comparable artisan product categories

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Calculate the fully-loaded cost per product SKU using current ingredient prices, then compare against current wholesale price to identify which products are now being sold below cost.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: open a retail outlet to reach end consumers directly
expand the product range to grow revenue
hire additional bakers to increase production capacity
reduce ingredient quality to lower costs

must_identify: ingredient cost increase not passed through
must_not_claim: revenue growth will resolve the margin problem
the business needs more clients
ideal_depth: identifies that specific products may now have negative contribution margin
notes that competitor pricing intelligence is needed before a price increase is designed

title: Personal Training Studio — Negative Unit Economics at Full Occupancy
business_context: A boutique personal training studio is running at full client capacity but consistently loses money each month despite strong member satisfaction and a waiting list.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — fitness and wellness sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner-operator of a personal training studio has 80 active members paying a flat monthly fee of $275 and operates at full capacity. Despite being fully booked the business loses approximately $3,200 per month. The owner believes the losses are temporary and will resolve as soon as a few more premium clients join.
symptoms: Business loses $3,200 per month despite operating at full capacity
Owner has not paid himself a market-rate wage for 11 months
Fixed costs include rent $7,200/month and equipment lease $1,800/month
Variable costs including scheduling software and insurance are $2,100/month
misleading_signals: Member satisfaction scores are high and there is a waiting list of 12 prospective clients
Three members have referred friends in the last month
The owner has received compliments on the quality of sessions
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Full monthly profit and loss statement showing every cost category
The breakeven number of members required at the current fee structure
Owner's own time value per hour versus billable session rate

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Calculate the total monthly cost including a market-rate owner wage, then divide by the current member count to determine the minimum monthly fee required to break even before considering growth.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: add more members beyond current capacity
hire a second trainer to serve the waiting list
invest in marketing to attract premium clients
take a loan to cover operating losses while growing

must_identify: fixed costs exceed revenue at full capacity
owner wage excluded from cost model
price increase required before adding capacity
must_not_claim: adding more clients will solve the loss
revenue growth will fix the unit economics without a price change
ideal_depth: calculates or estimates the minimum fee required to cover all costs including owner wage
identifies that the waiting list cannot be monetised without first fixing the unit economics

title: Accounting Practice — Referral Pipeline Collapse
business_context: A three-accountant SMB-focused accounting practice has seen new client referrals decline by 60% over two years with no active demand generation activity to replace lost pipeline.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — professional services sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a three-person accounting practice reports that the number of new clients joining each year has fallen significantly over two years. The practice has always relied on word-of-mouth referrals from existing clients and no formal marketing or lead generation activity has ever been implemented. Several long-standing referral sources have retired.
symptoms: New client referrals have fallen from 18 per year to 4 over two years
Three of the practice's five main referral sources have retired
No marketing, advertising, or lead generation activity has ever been used
Revenue has been sustained by existing client base but two long-term clients have also left
misleading_signals: Existing client retention remains high at 91%
Client satisfaction feedback is positive
The three accountants are at current capacity with existing workload
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Breakdown of where each of the last 20 new clients came from (referral source)
Capacity analysis showing how many additional clients the practice could onboard
Revenue concentration analysis showing the top five clients as a share of total revenue

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Map the source of every new client from the last three years to identify which referral relationships have become inactive and which new referral categories exist, before committing to any marketing spend.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: hire additional accountants to serve growth
open a second office location
reduce fees to win new clients on price
invest in paid digital advertising immediately

must_not_claim: the business needs to cut costs to survive
the pricing is too high for the market
ideal_depth: identifies that existing clients are at capacity so growth requires new demand
notes that referral source attrition is a specific and identifiable cause, not general market decline

title: Fine Dining Restaurant — Head Chef Departure Risk
business_context: A fine dining restaurant whose reputation and customer loyalty are built entirely on the head chef's personal style and culinary knowledge faces potential collapse if the chef departs, as no documented recipes or procedures exist.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — hospitality sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a fine dining restaurant reports that the head chef has been with the business for seven years and is the primary reason for the restaurant's reputation and loyal clientele. The owner has become aware that the chef is in discussions with a competitor. No recipes are documented, no other staff member can replicate the menu, and the owner has no culinary training.
symptoms: Head chef is in discussions with a competitor restaurant about a new role
All signature dishes exist only in the head chef's memory — no documented recipes
No other kitchen staff has been trained to lead service or replicate the menu
Owner has no culinary background and cannot cook the menu items
Bookings are fully committed three weeks ahead based on the chef's reputation
misleading_signals: Restaurant is fully booked three weeks in advance
Revenue has grown 24% over the past two years
Recent reviews specifically name the head chef and recommend the tasting menu
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: The chef's current employment contract including notice period and restraint of trade clauses
A list of which menu items and supplier relationships are exclusively managed by the chef
Assessment of whether any existing kitchen staff could be trained to lead service in the near term

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Negotiate immediately to document all recipes and preparation methods while the head chef is still employed, beginning with the highest-revenue signature dishes, and assess what contract retention incentive is feasible before the chef accepts another offer.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: hire additional front-of-house staff to improve customer experience
invest in marketing to grow the booking waitlist further
reduce menu prices to broaden the customer base
open a second restaurant location to grow the brand

must_not_claim: the restaurant needs more customers
the problem is pricing or cost structure
ideal_depth: identifies that the near-term risk is departure before knowledge transfer
notes that retention negotiation and documentation must happen simultaneously

title: Wedding Photography Studio — Post-Production Backlog Caps Bookings
business_context: A sole-operator wedding photography studio cannot take more bookings despite high demand because post-production editing creates a six-week backlog that the owner must process personally.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — creative services sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a wedding photography studio shoots 48 weddings per year and personally edits every set of photos. The editing backlog has grown to six weeks, causing some clients to complain about delivery times and the owner to decline new bookings. The owner shoots on weekends and edits on weekdays but cannot keep pace.
symptoms: Post-production editing backlog has reached six weeks — beyond the contractual delivery window
Owner is working 65 hours per week across shooting and editing
New booking enquiries are being declined because capacity is full
Two clients have complained about delayed delivery of their photos
misleading_signals: Enquiry volume is healthy with five new enquiries per week
Reviews on wedding platforms are strong with a 4.9 average rating
The business is fully booked twelve months ahead
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Time breakdown showing hours per wedding spent on shooting versus post-production editing
Whether any part of the editing process could be delegated to a trained assistant or outsourced editing service
Current contract terms specifying the delivery window committed to clients

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Calculate exactly how many hours of editing each wedding requires and what proportion of current workload could be delegated to an outsourced editing service or trained assistant, before accepting any new bookings.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: invest in new camera equipment to improve efficiency
increase pricing to reduce demand
hire a second photographer to shoot additional weddings
launch a marketing campaign to attract higher-value bookings

must_not_claim: the business needs more marketing
equipment upgrade will solve the problem
ideal_depth: identifies that editing is the constraint not shooting
notes that outsourced editing is a viable delegation option that should be costed

title: Dental Practice — Equipment Loan Repayment Exceeding Operating Capacity
business_context: A dental practice took a $280,000 equipment loan for a new dental chair and CBCT scanner but the $8,400 monthly repayment has consistently pushed the practice into a monthly cash deficit despite strong patient volumes.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — healthcare services sector

input_packet.business_description: The dentist-owner of a single-operator practice reports that cash shortfalls have worsened since taking a $280,000 equipment loan 22 months ago. Monthly repayments of $8,400 are being met but the practice consistently finishes each month with less cash than it started. The owner provided a personal guarantee on the loan and is concerned about covenant implications.
symptoms: Monthly cash deficit has persisted for 22 months since equipment loan was taken
Monthly debt service of $8,400 represents 13.6% of average monthly revenue
Operating cash before debt service has not been measured or compared to repayment
Personal guarantee provided on the loan creates personal financial risk
misleading_signals: Patient volumes are strong — the practice has a two-week appointment waitlist
The new scanner has enabled more complex procedures
Monthly revenue billings appear healthy at approximately $62,000
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Monthly operating cash flow before and after debt service for the past six months
Utilisation rate of the new equipment and incremental revenue it has generated
Full loan schedule including remaining term, covenants, and balloon payment dates

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Produce a monthly cash flow statement separating operating cash before debt service from loan repayment, to determine whether the underlying practice generates enough cash to support the debt or whether the loan has created a structural deficit.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: take a second loan to refinance the equipment debt
invest in marketing to grow patient volumes further
hire additional dental staff to increase throughput
reduce fee schedules to attract more patients

must_identify: operating cash before debt not established
loan proceeds insufficient to cover repayment
must_not_claim: the practice needs more patients to solve the cash problem
cutting staff costs will resolve the loan repayment issue
ideal_depth: identifies that the incremental revenue from the equipment must be compared to the repayment cost
notes that personal guarantee creates personal risk beyond business risk

title: B2B SaaS — Monthly Net Revenue Churn Destroying Growth
business_context: A small B2B SaaS product serving construction project managers is losing clients faster than it is acquiring them, with monthly net revenue churn of 4.2% eroding the entire value of new logo wins each month.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — technology sector

input_packet.business_description: The founder of a B2B SaaS product reports that despite consistently winning 3–4 new clients per month, the business has not grown its MRR over the past eight months. Three to four clients are cancelling subscriptions each month and the founder cannot identify a common reason. Onboarding completion rates are not tracked.
symptoms: Monthly net revenue churn of 4.2% means 50% annual client attrition
New logo wins of 3–4 per month are fully offset by 3–4 cancellations per month
MRR has been flat for eight consecutive months despite sales activity
Cancelling clients cite lack of time as the reason without specific product complaints
misleading_signals: The sales pipeline has consistently generated new logo wins each month
Product review scores remain positive on third-party review platforms
Several long-tenured clients have increased their seat counts
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Cancellation timing analysis showing when in the subscription lifecycle clients churn most frequently
Onboarding completion rate — what percentage of new clients complete the full product setup
Feature usage data showing which product features cancelling clients used versus retained clients

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Analyse the timing of every cancellation over the past 12 months to determine whether clients are churning early in the subscription or after extended use, as this determines whether the problem is onboarding or product-market fit.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: increase sales headcount to win more new logos
invest in paid advertising to grow the pipeline
reduce subscription pricing to improve retention
hire engineers to build additional features before diagnosing churn cause

must_identify: churn rate equals new acquisition rate
must_not_claim: the product needs more features to retain clients
the business needs more sales staff
ideal_depth: identifies that early-tenure churn is a different problem from late-tenure churn
notes that without usage data the churn cause cannot be distinguished from onboarding failure versus product-market fit

title: Commercial Cleaning Business — Quality Inconsistency Driving Contract Loss
business_context: A commercial office cleaning contractor has lost four contracts in the current year due to quality complaints, but new contract wins have kept revenue flat, masking the underlying retention problem.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — facilities management sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a commercial cleaning business reports that four contracts have been cancelled this year due to client complaints about inconsistent cleaning standards. Two of the cancellations cited specific incidents where a different cleaning team produced a noticeably lower standard than usual. No quality inspection process exists and client feedback is collected informally.
symptoms: Four contracts cancelled this year citing cleaning quality inconsistency
Two cancellations specifically referenced a change in the cleaning team assigned to the site
No quality inspection or checklist process exists — cleaners self-certify completion
Client complaints are handled informally with no written record
New contract wins have offset revenue from lost contracts masking the churn
misleading_signals: Total revenue has remained approximately stable due to new contract wins
Several long-standing clients have provided positive feedback
The owner personally audits one or two sites per week which pass without issue
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Log of every client complaint in the past 24 months with details of which cleaning team was on site
Staff assignment records showing which teams served which sites for the lost contracts
An independent audit of cleaning quality standards across all 18 active sites

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Cross-reference the four cancelled contracts with the staff assignment schedule to determine whether a specific team or teams are consistently associated with complaints, before implementing any business-wide quality programme.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: hire more cleaners to win additional contracts and replace lost revenue
invest in sales and marketing to grow the contract pipeline
reduce service pricing to retain at-risk clients
implement team bonus schemes before diagnosing the quality cause

must_not_claim: the business needs more clients
pricing is the reason for contract loss
ideal_depth: identifies that the quality problem may be team-specific rather than business-wide
notes that complaint and staff assignment records must be cross-referenced before any remediation

title: IT Managed Services — Labour Cost Scaling Ahead of Revenue
business_context: An IT managed services provider doubled its headcount over two years to serve growth but gross margin has fallen from 52% to 36% as labour costs have scaled faster than revenue and fixed-price contracts have been underpriced relative to actual service delivery time.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — technology services sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of an IT managed services provider reports that despite strong revenue growth from four to eight staff, the business is far less profitable than it was two years ago. The owner believes the declining margin is caused by staff wages increasing in the market. Fixed-price managed service contracts signed two years ago are still generating the same monthly revenue but now require more support hours per client as infrastructure complexity has grown.
symptoms: Gross margin has fallen from 52% to 36% as headcount grew from 4 to 8
Fixed-price managed service contracts have not been repriced in two years
Average hours per client per month have increased as client infrastructure has grown
Several new hires are at market rates 20–25% above the original team members
misleading_signals: Revenue has grown from $700K to $1.4M over two years
The client base has expanded from 12 to 22 clients
Several new enterprise clients have joined under long-term fixed-price agreements
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Time-tracking data showing actual hours per client per month versus contracted service hours
Gross margin by contract or client showing which agreements are profitable and which are loss-making
Analysis of whether new enterprise contracts were priced based on actual cost modelling or historical rates

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Produce a time-tracking analysis showing actual hours delivered per client per month and compare against the hours implied by each fixed-price contract to identify which agreements are currently loss-making.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: hire additional engineers to serve growth
invest in sales to win more enterprise contracts at current pricing
cut team salaries to restore margin
terminate underperforming staff to reduce the wage bill

must_identify: labour cost rising faster than revenue
must_not_claim: the business needs to grow revenue to fix the margin
cutting staff will restore profitability
ideal_depth: identifies that margin by contract must be measured before any pricing decision
notes that new enterprise contracts may have been priced on historical rates that no longer reflect actual delivery cost
